title: Temperature-dependent kinetic isotope effects in methane reactions with OH and Cl reshape atmospheric sink fractionation
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The abundances of stable isotopes in methane (CH
                    4
                    ) are used to distinguish fossil and biological emissions and to constrain the global methane budget. While these analyses require correction for isotopic fractionation occurring in methane’s atmospheric reactions, the temperature dependence of the kinetic isotope effects (KIEs) are poorly described and typically ignored. Here we combine density functional theory, Møller–Plesset perturbation theory, coupled-cluster calculations, and tunneling-corrected transition state theory to develop a first-principles description of the temperature-dependent KIEs for CH
                    4
                    and its isotopologues reacting with OH and Cl over the range 100 to 500 K which exhibit substantial and previously neglected temperature dependence. Incorporation of these KIEs into the EMAC chemistry–climate model yields systematically different effective atmospheric sink fractionation factors than those obtained using temperature-invariant values. The largest differences occur for chlorine oxidation in the cold upper troposphere and stratosphere, where methane isotope budgets are particularly sensitive to reactive halogens. We find a weak
                    13
                    C–D clumping anomaly and a strong D–D clumping anomaly, confirming earlier work and demonstrating that atmospheric oxidation produces substantial enrichment in Δ
                    12
                    CH
                    2
                    D
                    2
                    , and helping to reconcile source signatures with atmospheric observations. These results show that temperature-dependent KIEs are required for robust interpretation of methane isotopes in both contemporary and past atmospheres.

title: Unlocking the unparalleled paleoclimate record of Antarctic blue ice areas
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Ice uniquely provides direct samples of ancient atmosphere, enabling measurements of greenhouse gases contemporaneous to temperature reconstructions. Blue ice areas (covering 1% of the surface of Antarctica) hold a largely underexplored paleoclimate record that can extend beyond deep ice cores (that is, older than 1.5 My), covering periods in which global surface temperatures were similar to projected future temperatures. Blue ice areas expose ancient ice directly at the surface or at shallow depths due to net ablation and redirected ice flow, providing access to old ice at logistically reduced costs. However, the analysis and interpretation of blue ice samples is challenging, given the complex flow patterns in these regions that result in tilted layers, inversions and discontinuities in the stratigraphy, and complex ice–bedrock interactions. This paper presents a succinct review of state-of-the-art blue ice research, placed in the context of established ice core research, and argues that to advance the search for ancient ice, efforts in blue ice areas should focus on: i) collecting dated surface samples, ii) investigating the relationship between the age of the ice and other datable evidence, such as moraines, dust layers, meteorites, and exposed bedrock, and iii) developing models that can capture the typically disturbed or discontinuous stratigraphy. Together with advances in analytical techniques that address, for example, contamination and absolute dating, these efforts could lead to the recovery of the oldest ice on Earth, unravel warm climates of the past, and improve future climate change projections.

title: A two-dimensional molecular gearbox operated in a crystalline solid
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
Since the earliest artificial gears, parallel gearbox systems based on intermeshing two-dimensional (2D) networks of multiple gear units have served a fundamental role in macroscale mechanical devices through the correlated mechanical motion of multiple gears. However, the realization of molecular-level 2D gearbox machinery with correlated motion among multiple units remains highly challenging. Here, we report a molecular-level 2D gearbox in a crystal, formed through the supramolecular assembly of an Au(I)-complex rotor with tripodal triptycene and triadamantyl phosphine (Ad
                    3
                    P) rotators, connected via an ethynyl–Au(I) unit. Upon heating, the rotators within a 2D hexagonal gear network exhibit 120° site-exchange rotational motion in a correlated manner, as revealed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD),
                    2
                    H solid-state (SS) NMR spectroscopy, and time-resolved variable-temperature XRD measurements. In addition, density functional theory calculations provide insight into the energetic preference for correlated motion within the gear-network. This 2D intermolecular gearbox in the crystalline state represents a supramolecular platform in which the intermolecular gearing motion has a large impact on the bulk crystal, which could provide a bridge between molecular-level mechanical properties and macroscale SS physical functions.

title: Contrasting spatial homogeneity in atmospheric ice-nucleating particles from local to synoptic scales
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Ice-nucleating particles (INPs) play a critical role in regulating glaciation and precipitation formation in mixed-phase cloud (containing liquid and ice), yet their spatial variability across different scales remains poorly constrained. In this study, coordinated immersion freezing INP measurements from multiple sites during two campaigns in an urban–rural environment and complex mountainous terrain were used to investigate INP spatial distributions at tens-of-kilometer scales. At these scales, INP concentrations were generally spatially homogeneous during each campaign, indicating that single-site measurements can often represent surrounding areas. Occasional spatial differences were observed at warm activation temperatures (higher than −20 °C), ascribed to variations in heat-labile, likely biological INPs. Extending the analysis to the synoptic scale across multiple campaigns, warm-temperature INPs showed greater site-to-site differences, suggesting stronger influences from local or regional sources. In contrast, INPs active at colder temperatures showed much stronger spatial similarity between two inland continental sites separated by 800 km, revealing a broader regional coherence in this INP population. This was also observed at the coastal site, but only under continental air mass influence; the similarity weakened under marine air masses. These results suggest that cold-temperature INPs may reflect a broader INP background over continents such as that contributed by windblown dust. Our findings provide direct observational constraints on the representativeness of single-site INP measurements, which can help inform the strategy for representing variations in INP populations in atmospheric models.

title: Modulating chain conformations and hydrogen-bond dynamics at silica–rubber interfaces for enhanced energy dissipation in composites
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract:
The polymer–nanoparticle interphase is essential for fabricating high-performance nanocomposites, as it dictates mechanical properties through interfacial stress transfer and energy dissipation. However, engineering the buried interphases remains challenging due to the complex hierarchical structure and methodological limitations, particularly in silica–rubber systems where confined polymer chain conformation and hydrogen-bond dynamics are poorly resolved. Herein, a selective polymer-removal technique was developed to strip free and loosely bound polymer under extreme conditions, enabling TEM visualization of polymer chain-like interfacial features consistent with train-, loop-, and tail-like adsorption motifs in silica/silicone rubber nanocomposites. Correlative analysis combining STEM-EELS, high-resolution NMR, in situ variable-temperature IR, and 2D low-field NMR spectroscopy resolves hydrogen bonding between silica surface hydroxyls and silicone backbone oxygen atoms (Si-O-H···O-Si), which exhibit temperature-dependent behavior. Quantitative analysis reveals the strategic modulation of interphase layer thickness: As the apparent hydroxyl density of silica varied from 2.1 to 12.9 OH nm
                    −2
                    , the interphase thickness increased from 4.1 ± 0.8 nm to 13.2 ± 1.4 nm (9.5 mol% polymer phenyl); increasing the polymer phenyl content to 29.7 mol% further expands the layer to 23.4 ± 1.0 nm. Molecular dynamics simulations also suggest that higher silica surface hydroxyl density enhances multipoint adsorption of polymer chain, which promotes the formation of loop and train conformations. These confined chain arrangements are consistent with the reduced Arrhenius activation energy from 101 to 50 kJ mol
                    −1
                    measured by dynamic rheology, which facilitates interfacial chain mobility and hydrogen-bond exchange during deformation. These findings provide molecular-level insights for the rational design of polymer nanocomposites.

title: A deep-learning-boosted framework for quantum sensing with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond
source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: Keyword search for query
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a versatile quantum sensing platform for high sensitivity measurements of magnetic fields, temperature, and strain with nanoscale spatial resolution. A common bottleneck is the analysis of optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra, where target quantities are encoded in resonance features. Conventional nonlinear fitting is often computationally expensive, sensitive to initialization, and prone to failure at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Here we introduce a robust, efficient machine learning (ML) framework for real-time ODMR analysis based on a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN). The model performs direct parameter inference without initial guesses or iterative optimization, and is naturally parallelizable on graphics processing units (GPU) for high-throughput processing. We validate the approach on both synthetic and experimental datasets, showing improved throughput, accuracy, and robustness than standard nonlinear fitting, with the largest gains in the low-SNR regime. We further validate our methods in two representative sensing applications: diagnosing intracellular temperature changes using nanodiamond probes and widefield magnetic imaging of superconducting vortices in a high-temperature superconductor. This deep-learning inference framework enables fast and reliable extraction of physical parameters from complex ODMR data and provides a scalable route to real-time quantum sensing and imaging.

title: Ion‐Pair Mediation Enables Low‐Viscosity, Nonflammable Ternary Hybrid Electrolytes for High‐Voltage Aqueous Zinc Metal Batteries
source: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Aqueous zinc metal batteries (AZMBs) have garnered attention as promising energy storage devices owing to their intrinsic safety. However, the practical energy density of AZMBs is severely constrained by the narrow electrochemical window and sluggish kinetics inherent to conventional concentrated or viscous aqueous electrolytes. To address these limitations, a ternary hybrid system comprising a Zn(OTf) 2 /LiOTf dual‐salt matrix and low‐volume (5 vol.%) 1‐ethyl‐3‐methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (EMIMTFSI, abbreviated as EMT) ionic liquid is constructed. In the ternary system, EMIM + ‐TFSI − /OTf − ion pairs reconstruct the hydrogen‐bond network of the dual‐salt framework, thereby reducing bulk viscosity and broadening the electrochemical stability window to 2.76 V at low total salt concentrations. More importantly, these ion pairs undergo adsorption‐reduction‐anchoring to form an inner inorganic/outer organic bilayer, where OTf − /TFSI − decomposition generates a robust fluoride‐rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) that subsequently anchors EMIM + as a dynamic cationic shield. Consequently, the Zn//Zn symmetric cells achieve an outstanding lifespan of 3215 h at 1 mA cm −2 . Zn//MnO 2 ‐CNT battery demonstrates 88.21% capacity retention after 1100 cycles at 1 A g −1 within a high‐voltage range (0.8–2.0 V), and Zn//LiMn 2 O 4 battery exhibits a high discharge plateau of 1.86 V v s. Zn. This work offers a promising electrolyte design strategy for high‐voltage and long‐cycle‐life AZMBs.

title: Ion‐Pair Decoupler Tunes Solvation Chemistry for Room‐Temperature Polymer Electrolytes With Built‐In Flame Retardancy
source: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Solid‐state polymer electrolytes for high‐energy lithium‐metal batteries are severely constrained by low room‐temperature ionic conductivity. However, mainstream approaches focus on regulating the aggregate structure and flexibility of polymer chains while neglecting the ionic solvation microenvironment, which caps ionic conductivity gains at a marginal level. Here, an innovative ion‐pair decoupling strategy is proposed to reshape the Li + solvation chemistry within polymer matrices and to facilitate rapid ionic conduction. The ion‐pair decoupler, diethyl phosphoramidate, promotes the dissociation of lithium salt into a configuration dominated by solvent‐separated ion pairs by coordinating with Li + via its electron‐rich P = O groups and anchoring TFSI ‒ through hydrogen bond donors. Consequently, the ionic conductivity of the engineered electrolyte increases 24.6‐fold at 25°C. Li symmetric cells achieve stable cycling over 850 h, and Li||LiFePO 4 cells deliver a high‐capacity retention rate of 96.5% after 400 cycles at 25°C. Furthermore, the designed electrolyte exhibits excellent self‐extinguishing flame‐retardant properties by combining gas‐phase radical scavenging and condensed‐phase char‐forming mechanisms. Thus, a single molecular design simultaneously serves as an ion‐pair decoupler and an intrinsic flame retardant, establishing solvation‐chemistry tuning as a new paradigm for safe, room‐temperature solid polymer electrolytes.

title: In Situ Formation of Inorganic‐Rich Interphase via SiO2 Additive for High‐Performance Sodium Metal Batteries
source: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Sodium metal batteries (SMBs) are promising candidates for next‐generation high‐energy‐density storage systems, yet their practical application is hindered by dendritic growth and unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation. Herein, we report an in situ interfacial regulation strategy by introducing amorphous SiO 2 (a‑SiO 2 ) into Na metal anodes through an accumulative roll bonding process. We reveal that SiO 2 undergoes electrochemical reduction reaction with Na, generating SiO x (12 O—a beneficial inorganic SEI component that enhances interfacial ion transport and mechanical robustness. Furthermore, a‐SiO 2 exhibits superior interfacial reactivity and strong adsorption affinity toward fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC), promoting a NaF‐rich SEI that suppresses electrolyte decomposition. This synergetic inorganic‐rich SEI homogenizes Na deposition and accelerates ion diffusion kinetics. As a result, the Na/a‑SiO 2 symmetric cell achieves an ultralow overpotential of 24 mV at 0.5 mA cm −2 and stable cycling for over 1350 h. When paired with the Na 3 V 2 (PO 4 ) 2 O 2 F cathode, the full cell delivers excellent rate capability (73.9 mAh g −1 at 60 C) and cycling stability with 80% capacity retention after 8000 cycles at 20 C. This work establishes SiO 2 as a scalable and effective inorganic additive for tailoring SEI chemistry, offering a practical pathway toward high‐energy and durable SMBs.

title: Unified Grain‐Boundary and Electrode‐Interface Engineering Enables High‐Performance Magnesium‐Based Thermoelectrics
source: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT High‐performance thermoelectric devices require not only intrinsically efficient materials but also minimized transport losses across multiple interfaces during device integration. However, internal transport interfaces and external electrode contacts are typically optimized independently, creating a persistent challenge in translating material‐level advances into device‐level performance. Here we establish a unified interface engineering strategy in Bi‐rich Mg 3 (Sb,Bi) 2 thermoelectrics by using Nb as a multifunctional interface modifier. In Mg 3 Sb 0.7 Bi 1.3 , Nb‐rich internal interfaces regulate grain‐boundary carrier transport, while Nb foils provide chemically stable and low‐resistance electrode contacts. First‐principles calculations and atomic‐scale characterization reveal that the Bi‐rich composition suppresses extensive Nb‐related reactions while enabling electronically favorable confined interfaces. Nb incorporation increases the weighted mobility to 315.6 cm 2 ·V −1 ·s −1 and achieves a room‐temperature zT above 0.8, while Nb foil contacts yield an intrinsic contact resistivity of 1.8 µΩ·cm 2 . Integrating Nb‐engineered n‐type Mg 3 Sb 0.7 Bi 1.3 with p‐type MgAgSb enables Mg‐based thermoelectric modules with a conversion efficiency of 3.8% at Δ T = 100 K and a maximum cooling temperature difference of 82.7 K at a hot‐side temperature of 373 K. This work establishes a general interface design principle for thermoelectrics, demonstrating that interface modifiers for bulk transport optimization can also serve as electrode‐contact materials to bridge the gap between high‐performance materials and practical devices.

title: In Situ Polymerized Interfaces Enable Robust and High‐Performance Dry‐Coating Electrodes
source: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: ABSTRACT Dry‐coating electrode technology eliminates the use of toxic N‐methyl‐2‐pyrrolidone and offers a promising route for sustainable battery manufacturing. However, its practical implementation remains limited by the weak interfacial mechanics among rigid cathode particles, polytetrafluoroethylene nanofibers, and conductive carbon additives. These fragile interfaces reduce mechanical robustness and interfacial stability, thereby compromising both processability and electrochemical performance. Here, we report an in situ polymerization strategy using a polymerizable deep eutectic liquid additive, which forms an adhesive polymer network upon photopolymerization, thereby reinforcing contact among electrode components and improving electrode robustness. The resulting dry‐coating LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 (NCM811) electrodes exhibit a 55% increase in elongation at break and deliver a reversible specific capacity of 121 mAh g −1 at 5 C with a mass loading of 10 mg cm −2 . A 3.77 Ah Li||NCM811 pouch cell achieves maximum cell‐level energy and power densities of 412 Wh kg −1 and 574 W kg −1 , respectively. In addition, a 0.60 Ah graphite||NCM811 pouch cell retains 70% of its capacity after 870 cycles. Our results establish in situ polymerization as a viable route for mechanically robust, high‐performance dry‐coating electrodes.

Beyond generation capabilities alone, augmenting the model's training dataset to include the full electrode thickness preserves calendering-induced through-plane features, improving the tortuosity factor of produced microstructures. Generated electrodes match the performance of experimentally resolved LIB cathodes under 3D simulations, enabling high-throughput exploration of process–structure–performance relationships. More in article number e71418, Alejandro A. Franco and co-workers.

title: Decoupling Thermodynamic and Kinetic Moisture Instability Reveals a Critical Humidity Threshold for Sodium Thiophosphate Solid Electrolyte (Adv. Energy Mater. 44/2026)
source: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
abstract: Moisture Tolerance In article number e71467, Chengcheng Fang and co-workers reveal that moisture stability in Na3PS4 is governed by competition between dehydration and hydrolysis. Under limited moisture exposure, thermal treatment removes absorbed water and largely restores ionic conductivity, whereas severe exposure promotes irreversible hydrolysis. These findings establish a kinetic basis for moisture tolerance and recovery in sulfide solid electrolytes.

title: Fa‐Jie Chen
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: "My long-term goal is to develop "click" methods for peptide cyclization and library construction for high-throughput screening and drug discovery… If I were a piece of lab equipment, I would be a thin-layer chromatography (TLC) plate, because I could be the eyes for chemists to see what is going on in organic reactions…" Find out more about Fa-Jie Chen in his Introducing… Profile.

title: Learning beyond rigid manipulation with hybrid soft-rigid robots
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Rigid-soft robot hybrids promise to unite the precision and repeatability of rigid manipulators with the compliance and adaptability of soft structures. Yet, full-fledged rigid-soft manipulators remain largely unexplored, in part because the intelligence required to exploit this combination is still missing. Here, we introduce a hybrid robotic system obtained by the series interconnection of a rigid arm and a soft manipulator, and systematically examine its ability to perform both established and previously inaccessible manipulation tasks. We show that a tailored imitation learning algorithm–generally applicable to this class of hybrid systems–leverages the complementary roles of rigid precision and soft embodiment to acquire manipulation skills and generalize them in a single shot across task variations. As a result, the system matches or exceeds the performance of rigid robots in classical tasks such as stacking, while enabling qualitatively new behaviors, including grasping objects through narrow openings.

title: Cation Pinning toward High-Concentration Formic Acid Fuel Cells
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Despite the high theoretical energy density of concentrated formic acid, direct formic acid fuel cells (DFAFCs) incorporating conventional nanoparticle or emerging single-atom anodes exhibit a precipitous power loss as fuel concentration scales. While CO poisoning is traditionally blamed, we show that this limitation is governed by interfacial acid–base kinetics. By implementing a cation-pinning strategy via rare-earth oxide-modified Rh single-atom sites, we stabilize OH– from water dissociation through interfacial ionic anchoring to trigger localized pH inversion. This modulation leads to the preferential enrichment of interfacial formate, identified here as the primary reactive species. Consequently, Dy2O3–Rh/NC delivers a mass activity 641-fold higher than that of nanoparticle benchmarks. The resulting anode achieves an exceptional peak power density of 375 mW cm–2, surpassing commercial Pd/C across all concentrations. This work establishes precision ionic management as a versatile approach to breaking performance limits in multiphase catalysis.

title: Rh2C3− Cluster-Driven Nitrogen Activation: Trapping a High-Energy Intermediate
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Converting inert and globally abundant molecules such as N2 into useful chemicals is central to sustainable energy and environmental chemistry. Herein, we investigate the gas-phase reaction of the Rh2C3− anion with N2 using mass spectrometry, anion photoelectron spectroscopy, and quantum chemical calculations. The experimental spectra of Rh2C3− and Rh2C3N2− exhibit closely similar features, indicating a preserved electronic core upon N2 attachment. Theoretical analysis further reveals that the end-on N2 adsorption complex is a trapped high-energy intermediate whose subsequent transformation is prevented by an activation barrier that necessitates additional energy input, and that this complex exhibits superior performance in the coconversion of diverse energy-bearing gas molecules. Furthermore, the subsequent application of oriented external electric fields provides a nondestructive and continuously adjustable means of modifying the intrinsic barrier heights, thereby effectively switching the reaction mechanism. These findings elucidate the complex reaction network of Rh2C3− with N2, establish a reliable spectroscopic fingerprint for identifying isomeric intermediates, and provide fundamental insights into electronic control strategies for catalytic nitrogen activation.

title: A Bioinspired Thiolate-Bridged Diiron System for Functionally Replicating Hydrazine Dehydrogenase and Its Efficient Electrocatalytic Hydrazine Oxidation
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Hydrazine dehydrogenase (HDH) catalyzes the oxidation of hydrazine (N2H4) to dinitrogen (N2) as the final step of anaerobic ammonium oxidation, an essential process in closing the nitrogen cycle. Despite extensive biochemical studies, the detailed mechanism of HDH at a molecular level remains elusive. An increasing number of studies indicate that the hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR) is also central to direct hydrazine fuel cells. However, known electrocatalysts for HzOR are predominantly heterogeneous systems, while molecular electrocatalysts are still scarce, especially those inspired by biological HDH. This scarcity not only limits mechanistic understanding but also hinders the development of efficient and tunable catalysts. To tackle these challenging issues, we sought inspiration from the biological HDH system, wherein multiple iron-containing heme subunits cooperatively promote efficient HzOR with the assistance of surrounding sulfur-bearing cysteine residues. Integrating these key features, we selected the thiolate-bridged diiron complex [Cp*Fe(μ-SEt)(MeCN)]2[PF6]2 (1, Cp* = η5-C5Me5) for functionally replicating HDH. Treatment of 1 with N2H4 induces disproportionation to afford the active diazene (N2H2) species, which can be captured by the diiron cooperative platform to yield [Cp*Fe(μ-SEt)2(cis-μ-η1:η1-HN=NH)FeCp*][PF6] (2). In the presence of appropriate electron and proton acceptors, complex 2 undergoes a two-electron oxidation, leading to N2 release and the regeneration of 1. Remarkably, both complexes 1 and 2 serve as efficient molecular electrocatalysts for HzOR. This diiron molecular system not only achieves the functional replication of HDH involving a key N2H2 intermediate but also establishes a bioinspired design strategy for developing multimetal cooperative electrocatalysts toward efficient HzOR.

title: Revisiting the Biosynthetic Cyclization of Indole Sesquiterpene Alkaloids: Proposal of a Spiro -Indolenine Pathway and Synthesis of Prelecanindole
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Indole sesquiterpene and indole diterpene alkaloids constitute a distinctive class of natural products characterized by complex polycyclic ring architectures and diverse potent biological activities. In indole sesquiterpenes, the characteristic indole-containing pentacyclic skeleton is biosynthesized from 3-farnesylindole through epoxidation followed by a sequential cationic cyclization. Although the cyclization enzyme has been identified, the details of its cyclization mechanism remain unclear. Here, we propose a new biosynthetic mechanism involving a spiro-indoleninium intermediate, which contrasts with the long-standing mechanism proposed in the 1970s that proceeds via a tertiary-to-secondary carbocation rearrangement. We demonstrated the feasibility of this new mechanism by means of density functional theory (DFT) calculations, which do not support the conventional mechanism and also by chemical emulation: the putative spiro-indolenine intermediate was synthesized from two fragments through stereoselective cyclopropanation as a key reaction and subsequently converted to prelecanindole, a common biosynthetic intermediate of indole sesquiterpene alkaloids, under mild acidic conditions.

title: Single-Atom Cerium Unlocks Efficient Hydrogen Spillover within Nonreducible Zeolites through a Proton–Electron Relay
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Hydrogen spillover connects hydrogen activation with spatially separated catalytic functions, yet engineering efficient hydrogen transport through nonreducible zeolites remains an outstanding challenge owing to the absence of intrinsic pathways for coupled proton–electron transfer. Here, we show that isolated cerium atoms incorporated into Pt/USY transform the zeolite from a passive support into an active medium for solid-state hydrogen transport. In situ spectroscopy, isotopic tracing, and theoretical calculations reveal that atomically dispersed Ce species dynamically generate localized hydroxyl groups and oxygen vacancies that cooperatively establish a proton–electron relay, substantially lowering the kinetic barrier for hydrogen migration through zeolitic micropores. The resulting enhancement in hydrogen spillover extends hydrogen delivery to spatially remote Brønsted acid sites, suppresses coke formation, and significantly improves polyolefin hydrocracking stability. These findings establish hydrogen transport as a tunable design parameter in bifunctional zeolite catalysis and provide a general strategy for engineering hydrogen-transfer pathways in nonreducible porous materials.

title: Redox-Window-Guided Metal Node Editing of Copper Metal–Organic Frameworks for Recyclable Heterogeneous Cu(I) Catalysis
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Cu(I) catalysts are central to many bond-forming reactions, but integrating Cu(I) sites into recyclable porous solids remains difficult because Cu(I) is easily oxidized, over-reduced, or leached. Here, we report redox-window-guided metal node editing as an oxidation-state-programming strategy that converts hydrolytically fragile Cu(II)3BTC2 into a hydrolytically stable mixed-valence Cu(I/II) MOF catalyst. Phenolic reductants are selected by matching their oxidation potentials to the Cu(II)–to–Cu(I) window of Cu(II)3BTC2, enabling proton-coupled, inner-sphere single-electron transfer at Cu paddlewheel nodes. Hydroquinone gives the most controlled material, [p-Ph(OH)2]-Cu3BTC2, containing 33.4% Cu(I), ship-in-a-bottle [Cu(MeCN)4]+ complexes, mesopores, and enhanced stability under humid, acidic, and basic conditions. As a heterogeneous catalyst for hydrative amide synthesis, [p-Ph(OH)2]-Cu3BTC2 affords 92% yield, negligible Cu leaching, five-cycle recyclability, and the highest turnover number among compared Cu(I) catalysts.

title: Hydrogen-Bond Network-Assisted Ethylene and Hydrogen Photosynthesis from Methane over Isolated Ir Active Sites under Ambient Conditions
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Direct conversion of methane to ethylene (DCM) is an attractive yet formidable challenge due to the difficult C–H activation and uncontrollable C–C coupling process. Herein, we report a hydrogen-bond network-assisted ethylene and H2 photosynthesis from methane over oxygen-vacancy-enriched TiO2-supported single Ir atoms (Ir1/TiO2–Ov) under ambient conditions. The Ir-induced lattice distortion drives spontaneous hydrolysis under humid conditions, generating a hydroxylated surface that endows coordinatively unsaturated Ir sites to activate the first methane molecule without light irradiation. Upon photoexcitation, surface hydroxyls are oxidized into dangling oxygen species (*O) on Ti sites, which promote the dehydrogenation of *CH3 to *CH2. In synergy with the Ir site, the adjacent *O species activate a second CH4 molecule and finally direct selective C–C coupling to form C2H4. Meanwhile, methane-derived protons migrate through the hydrogen-bond network via a Grotthuss mechanism to produce H2. The Ir1/TiO2–Ov catalyst achieves the production of ethylene (14.3 ± 0.7 μmol•gcat–1•h–1) and H2 (28.4 ± 1.2 μmol•gcat–1•h–1) for at least 210 h at 25 °C and atmospheric pressure under light irradiation. Our findings establish a hydrogen-bond network-assisted strategy for methane C–H activation and selective C–C and H–H coupling.

title: Ligand-Controlled Chemodivergent β-Methylene C(sp3)–H Heteroarylation of Aliphatic Acids
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Achieving ligand-controlled chemodivergence in C–H activation is still difficult because several competing reaction pathways are available when multiple C–H bonds are present. We describe a Pd(II)-catalyzed, chemodivergent β-methylene C(sp3)–H heteroarylation of free aliphatic acids in which two distinct classes of bidentate pyridone ligands each deliver a different product. These two ligands also overcome a long-standing inhibitory effect of heteroaryl iodides, demonstrating the potential of this protocol to serve as a general C(sp3)–C(sp2) coupling method using readily available aliphatic acids as the alkylating partner. Mechanistic experiments and DFT analyses reveal that π–π stacking between the quinoline motif and the heteroaryl ring lowers the barrier for rotation of the carbon–palladium bond, favoring protodepalladation to the reductive Heck product, whereas the oxime ether ligand lacks this interaction and steers the key intermediate toward β-H elimination to give the oxidative Heck product.

title: Targeting chemotherapy-induced CD200 via a nucleoside-enhanced nanocarrier for cancer immunochemotherapy
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has transformed cancer therapy, yet its efficacy is frequently undermined by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. In addition, the immune-related toxicities restrict combination therapy targeting several immune checkpoints. Here, we identify chemotherapy-induced CD200 upregulation as a stress-adaptive resistance mechanism that reinforces tumor immune evasion under treatment pressure. Leveraging a tumor-restricted, nucleoside-enhanced nanocarrier, we achieve spatially selective silencing of tumor-intrinsic CD200, thereby reprogramming the tumor immune microenvironment, enhancing antitumor efficacy, and enabling effective combination with PD-1 blockade. Importantly, this strategy minimizes the colitis exacerbation associated with systemic CD200/PD-1 dual blockade in a DSS-induced susceptibility model, suggesting its potential to preserve immune homeostasis while reducing immune-related toxicity. Together, our findings establish CD200 as a context-dependent immune resistance node and demonstrate a nanotechnology-based framework for precise and safe immune checkpoint modulation.

title: Unlocking Fast and Durable Li + Transport Beyond Polymer Segmental Dynamics for High‐Rate and Long‐Life Lithium Metal Batteries
source: Advanced Energy Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Polymer electrolytes are promising for safe lithium metal batteries, yet their ionic transport is fundamentally limited by polymer segmental dynamics, hindering fast charging and long‐term cycling. Here, we report a microphase‐separated quasi‐solid‐state polymer electrolyte that enables rapid and durable Li + transport through localized coordination regulation. Covalently tethered pyrrolidinium ionic liquid moieties promote lithium salt dissociation while suppressing anion migration, whereas in situ generated thioether linkages weaken Li + ‐polymer interactions and enhance chain flexibility. Their synergistic integration creates a dynamic coordination environment that facilitates low‐energy Li + hopping between adjacent coordination sites, substantially reduced ion transport dependence on polymer segmental dynamics. As a result, the optimized electrolyte delivers a room‐temperature ionic conductivity of 1.13 mS cm −1 , a high Li + transference number of 0.82, and a low activation energy of 0.17 eV. The accelerated and homogeneous Li + transport promotes stable lithium deposition, enabling lithium metal batteries with 97.9% capacity retention after 2500 cycles at 10C and stable operation for 400 cycles at 5C even at 120°C. More broadly, this work demonstrates a viable pathway to break the conventional trade‐off between polymer processability and ion‐transport kinetics, offering a new paradigm for high‐performance solid‐state lithium metal batteries.

title: Tandem Solar Cells Based on Si and Stable Cu(In,Ga)S 2 With Efficiency Beyond the Bottom Cell
source: Advanced Energy Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Tandem solar cells require stable, highly efficient top cells with a band gap above 1.6 eV. We present a semitransparent solar cell with an efficiency of 15.52% and an open‐circuit voltage of 1.014 V, based on an environmentally stable sulfide chalcopyrite absorber and ITO back contact. Solar cells are prepared by industrially scalable processes of co‐evaporation, sputter and atomic layer deposition. The progress in efficiency is achieved by alloying with small amounts of Ag (less than 10% of Cu replaced by Ag). Optimum amount of Ag alloying is shown to depend on the amount of Cu‐excess during absorber growth. Ag alloying leads to larger grains, avoids high Ga phases, and reduces non‐radiative recombination, which improves open circuit voltage. Whether the reduction in non‐radiative recombination is due to an increase in net doping or due to a longer minority carrier lifetime appears to depend on the Cu‐excess during process. The efficiency of the top cell remains stable over several months’ storage in a non‐controlled atmosphere. We combine this new top cell in a tandem cell with both Si and CuInSe 2 bottom cells, in both cases, the efficiency beyond the bottom cell alone by between 2.5% and 5% absolute.

title: Disagreements in global urban growth projections amplify uncertainties in deforestation and carbon emissions
source: Scientific community and society : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Global urbanization is profoundly reshaping 21st-century land systems, yet its future trajectory remains highly uncertain. Existing projections exhibit divergent urban growth patterns even under identical socioeconomic scenarios. Here, by synthesizing six urban growth projections, we reveal substantial disagreements in the extent and location of urban growth by 2100. These disagreements are amplified by land-system feedbacks, driving cross-dataset variation in urban-induced deforestation (1.75–4.91 million km2) through direct forest conversion and indirect cropland displacement, assuming lost production is compensated by cropland expansion elsewhere. The associated emissions exhibit an absolute range of 29 to 76 GtCO2 by 2100. Across 100 countries, this range accounts for an average of 3% of unconditional Nationally Determined Contribution emission budgets, reaching 26% in specific countries. Our findings establish cross-dataset disagreement as an important source of uncertainty in land and climate assessments, highlighting the need for robust spatial planning across plausible urban futures.

title: Interphasial Li + Flux Engineering via Anchoring Vertically Oriented Fluorinated Covalent Organic Frameworks Toward Long‐Cycling Li‐Metal Batteries
source: Advanced Energy Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Unstable solid electrolyte interphases and uncontrollable Li‐dendrite growth largely hamper the practical application of metallic Li anode in rechargeable batteries. Constructing a reliable and steady Li interphase is critical to promote commercialization of Li‐metal batteries. In this study, we propose to directionally anchor 2D fluorinated covalent organic frameworks on Li metal to build artificial solid electrolyte interphases, aiming to homogenize and accelerate the interphasial Li + flux and regulate uniform Li plating/stripping. Theoretical calculations reveal that active fluorine sites with negative electrostatic potential facilitate fast LiTFSI dissociation and strong Li + adsorption, and oriented 2D channels with low diffusion energy barrier endow high Li + flux and fast Li + transport. The obtained interphase has a homogeneously amorphous structure with high mechanical elasticity and thermodynamic stability, exhibiting high compatibility with metallic Li and enabling excellent electrochemical properties. Consequently, its symmetrical cell demonstrates an ultralong cycle life over 1300 h. When paired with commercial cathodes, LiFePO 4 cell and LiNi 0.5 Co 0.2 Mn 0.3 O 2 cell demonstrate a cycle‐life of 335 and 228 at 5 C, respectively. Notably, 1 Ah LiNi 0.5 Co 0.2 Mn 0.3 O 2 //modified Li pouch‐cell exhibits a long cycle‐life over 325 at 1 C. This study offers an effective method for enhancing Li metal interphase stability of high‐energy‐density Li‐metal batteries.

title: Biomimetic Reversible Phase Transition in Scandium‐Based Metal Halides for Environment‐Interactive Information Security
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Inspired by the dynamic adaptive coloration of cephalopods, mimicking their reversible, environment‐interactive response behavior is essential for biomimetic material design. The high color purity, multi‐wavelength tunability, long luminescence lifetimes, excellent stability, and reversible stimuli‐responsive behavior of lanthanide‐based emitters render them indispensable in biomimetic camouflage, intelligent sensing, electronic skin, and adaptive optical materials. In this study, we develop a biomimetic system based on zero‑dimensional Cs 4 ScCl 7 ·H 2 O and its interconvertible counterpart Cs 2 ScCl 5 ·H 2 O via a simple “dissolve–dry” method. Bidirectional phase transitions are achieved by facile alternating ScCl 3 and CsCl treatment. Density functional theory calculations rationalize this phase selectivity and the resultant color switching via a kinetic–thermodynamic competition. Doping with antimony and lanthanide enables self‐trapped exciton emission, downshifting luminescence, and upconversion luminescence, with the capability of reversible cyclic switching upon structural transformation. Utilizing this capability of reversible color switching in response to external stimuli, two complementary applications are demonstrated: physically unclonable function labels for medicines anti‑counterfeiting, and stimuli‑responsive luminescence for dynamic information encryption (integrating dynamic encoding with a secret‐sharing hierarchical authorization framework). Together, these strategies achieve zero‑error authentication and strong cloning resistance. This work establishes rare earth‑based low‑dimensional metal halides as a biomimetic, environment‑interactive system for next‑generation, highly secure anti‑counterfeiting and encryption technologies.

title: Polarity‐Directed Assembly of in‐Plane Oriented Covalent Organic Framework Films on Substrates
source: Angewandte Chemie International Edition
abstract: ABSTRACT Two‐dimensional (2D) covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs) are promising crystalline porous materials for optoelectronic applications; however, controlled growth of COF thin films on substrates remains a significant challenge. Here, we develop a polarity‐directed solution assembly strategy for the fabrication of 2D COF thin films on various substrates. This approach leverages polarity‐driven solvent–molecule interactions to regulate precursor assembly and oriented polymerization, successfully yielding in‐plane oriented COF films with controllable thickness, smooth surface morphology, and abundant nitrogen active sites. When these films are used as templates for perovskite growth, the resulting heterojunction interfaces effectively passivate buried interfacial defects and suppress non‐radiative recombination. Integrated into light‐emitting diodes (LED), the devices achieve a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 30.88%, a peak luminance of 1.7 × 10 5 cd/m 2 , and an operational half‐lifetime (T 50 ) of 12.74 h at an initial luminance of 9206 cd/m 2 (equivalent to >6238 h at 100 cd/m 2 ), surpassing most previously reported counterparts. This work opens a new molecular regulation avenue toward the preparation of highly oriented COF films for versatile optoelectronic applications.

title: Dynamic B–OH intermediates enable photocatalytic conversion of CO2 into formic acid
source: Earth and environmental sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Remediating of flue gas pollutants and the mitigation of carbon emissions represent two interconnected yet often conflicting challenges in environmental management. Here we report a borane-assisted photocatalytic system that achieves synergistic co-conversion of CO2, NOx, and SO2 from flue gas into valuable liquid products-formic, nitric, and sulfuric acids-with near-complete selectivity and high stability. Central to this process is the in situ generation of dynamic B-OH intermediates at the borane-catalyst interface, which serve as proton relays to activate water-derived protons for CO2 reduction while promoting reactive oxygen species for pollutant oxidation. This mechanism enables approximately 77.02% of the hydrogen in formic acid to originate from water. The system demonstrates broad applicability across diverse photocatalysts and borane reagents, and exhibits sustained performance under simulated flue gas conditions. Our work establishes a sustainable and economically viable pathway for integrated carbon and pollutant valorization, offering a scalable strategy toward circular carbon economies.

title: Stepwise Assembly of a Lavandulyl Moiety on Flavonoids Enabled by a 2″-Prenyltransferase
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Lavandulylated flavonoids contain a characteristic branched C10 moiety, and the enzymatic basis underlying its biosynthesis remains poorly understood. Here, we elucidate the complete biosynthetic pathway of the lavandulylated flavonoid kurarinone from naringenin in the medicinal plant Sophora flavescens. The pathway involves four sequential steps, 8-prenylation, 2′-hydroxylation, 2″-prenylation, and 5-O-methylation, catalyzed by Sf8PT, SfF2′H, Sf2″PT, and Sf5OMT, respectively. Sf2′′PT represents the first characterized flavonoid 2′′-prenyltransferase (PT), catalyzing a second prenylation on the pre-existing prenyl side chain to complete the assembly of the branched lavandulyl moiety. The activity of Sf2″PT strictly depends on prior 2′-hydroxylation, establishing a defined order of enzymatic modifications that enables this noncanonical prenylation reaction. Ancestral sequence reconstruction and mutagenesis demonstrated that an inactive ancestral enzyme could be converted into functional 8PT or 2′′PT variants through one or seven amino acid substitutions, respectively. Collectively, this work establishes the enzymatic basis for stepwise lavandulyl moiety assembly and provides a framework for the enzymatic construction and engineering of branched prenylated natural products.

title: A quasi-particle theory for the dynamics of polycatenated architected materials
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Architected materials derive unusual mechanical responses from geometry rather than mostly by their chemistry. Polycatenated architected materials (PAMs), composed of interlinked rigid units, have been shown to display hybrid solid–fluid behaviors. Frequency-sweep rheological experiments have revealed a transition from strong shear thinning at low frequencies to pronounced shear thickening above a critical frequency. Because neighboring PAM units are connected, rather than freely rearranging, conventional granular theories do not readily explain their behavior. Here, we develop a one-dimensional analytical model to capture the frequency-response of PAMs based on a quasi-particle description. Quasi-particles are defined as segments of PAMs that are either fully stretched or fully compressed. Modeling their interactions produces an effective viscosity that captures both asymptotic scaling laws and the critical frequency. These predictions agree quantitatively with simulations and experiments. Our results reveal that PAM’s frequency-dependent response arises from competing effects between dissipation and inertia. More broadly, our results establish an analytical foundation for understanding the dynamics of PAMs and provide design principles for tuning their responses.

title: The nature of the phase transition in VO2 B-phase and a quantum entanglement perspective
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The well-known metal-to-insulator transition in rutile/monoclinic VO2 has been understood as a correlation-enhanced Peierls phenomenon. The lesser-known B-polymorph exhibits a similar resistivity jump, assumed to arise from an analogous transition. However, unlike rutile/monoclinic VO2, here the transition is isostructural, with dimers persisting both above and below the transition, challenging established interpretations. Here, we show that the phase transition in the B-polymorph is qualitatively different. Despite high conductivity and finite spectral weight at the chemical potential, the high-temperature phase lacks standard metallic screening and Drude peaks. Our theoretical analysis reveals that while the low-temperature insulating phase is driven by both Peierls and Mott physics, the high-temperature state is an anomalous insulator whose apparent metallicity arises from incoherent in-gap states that mimic a metal. We relate this unusual growth of incoherent states to temperature-dependent intra-dimer charge transfers. Finally, we propose a unified framework using an Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen-like quantum-entanglement measure to characterize and distinguish between different VO2 phases hosting dimers.

title: Impact-stiffening materials modulated by host–guest interactions in polypseudorotaxanes
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The development of high-performance impact-stiffening materials is critical for applications spanning personal protection to military defense. Conventional designs of such materials relying on strong noncovalent interactions often face a strength–toughness trade‑off. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a strategy that utilizes the dynamic threading–dethreading kinetics of host–guest complexes in polypseudorotaxanes to fabricate impact‑stiffening materials. Unlike binding‑strength‑governed designs, this approach is governed by kinetic mismatch between the dethreading time of the macrocycle and the external deformation time. This kinetic control decouples the static compliance from the dynamic stiffening threshold, enabling pronounced impact‑stiffening even with a modest solution‑phase binding constant. Under low shear rates, the macrocycles gradually slide from the polymer backbone, preserving flexibility. Upon high-speed impact, the dethreading of host–guest complexes cannot occur within the ultrashort loading window of deformation, kinetically freezing the network and increasing the storage modulus by 48‑fold (0.1–100 Hz, 25 °C). The material also exhibits self-healing, reprocessability, and strong adhesion. This work demonstrates rate-dependent host–guest disassembly as a design principle for adaptive impact-protective materials.

title: Extending frequency metrology to increasingly complex molecules: SI-traceable sub-Doppler mid-IR spectroscopy of trioxane
source: Physical sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Bringing increasingly complex polyatomic molecules within reach of precision measurement experiments opens new prospects ranging from Earth sciences and astrophysics, to metrology and quantum sciences. Here, we demonstrate sub-Doppler mid-IR spectroscopic measurements of, to our knowledge, the largest molecule to date, 1,3,5-trioxane, (H2CO)3, in its ν5 CO stretching mode. To this end, we use an ultra-high-resolution ~10.3 µm spectrometer based on a sub-Hz quantum cascade laser remotely calibrated against state-of-the-art primary frequency standards via a metrology-grade fibre link. We perform saturated absorption spectroscopy at low pressure with ~100 kHz resolution. This allows measuring the absolute frequency of hundreds of rovibrational transitions at unprecedented statistical and systematic uncertainties for such a complex species, as low as 4.6 kHz and 6.2 kHz respectively. In addition to providing new spectroscopic information on trioxane, our work extends frequency metrology methodologies to ever larger molecular systems, confirming the potential of our technologies for bringing increasingly complex species within reach of ultra-precise measurement experiments.

title: Hybrid simulations of nonlinear zonal flow generation by multi- n toroidal Alfvén eigenmo...
source: Nuclear Fusion - latest papers
abstract: In burning plasmas, zonal flows (ZFs) excited by toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes (TAEs) play a crucial role in improving energy confinement. In this work, strong self-generated ZFs are analyzed in a multi- TAE system through nonlinear hybrid simulations using the CLT-K code, where the ZFs are driven by self-beat interactions of TAEs. The results show that the strong ZFs dominate the nonlinear stage and significantly suppress the TAE activity. The ZF mode structures consist of the and harmonics, and are directly correlated with the spatial structures of TAEs. Further analysis of the ZF kinetic energy evolution demonstrates that a finite residual between the Reynolds and Maxwell stresses, arising from toroidal geometry, enables net energy transfer from TAEs to ZFs, with an additional contribution from the energetic particles (EPs) pressure response. In addition, the linear Lorentz force contributes either to ZF pumping or damping depending on the stage of the evolution. Strong ZF generation is favored in regimes with high EP pressure and low viscosity. A self-regulating process is identified: stronger TAEs drive stronger ZFs, which in turn regulates the TAE activity. These findings provide both numerical and physical insights into the role of ZFs in regulating EP-driven instabilities in tokamak plasmas.

title: Cyanoethyl Cellulose‐Mediated Polymer Electrolyte With Fast Li + Transport and Stable Interface for Long‐Cycle Solid‑State Lithium Metal Batteries
source: Advanced Energy Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Solid polymer electrolytes (SPEs) are promising for solid‐state lithium metal batteries (SSLMBs) owing to their safety, flexibility, and processability. However, simultaneously achieving fast Li + transport and stable electrode/electrolyte interface remains a great challenge. Herein, a cyanoethyl cellulose (CEC)‐mediated polymer–polymer modulation strategy is proposed to construct high‐performance Poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF)/lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) composite electrolyte (PL‐CEC). Functional CEC effectively disrupts the ordered stacking structure of PVDF chains, while abundant polar cyano groups in CEC precisely modulate the local Li + coordination environment, promote Li salt dissociation and fast Li + migration. The optimized PL‐CEC exhibits high room‐temperature ionic conductivity and superior Li + transference number. Moreover, PL‐CEC stabilizes both electrode interfaces, suppressing Li dendrite growth and high‐voltage electrolyte decomposition. Consequently, Li|PL‐CEC|Li cells realize stable Li plating/stripping for 1400 h at 0.4 mA cm −2 and 0.4 mAh cm −2 . Li|PL‐CEC|LiFePO 4 full cells retain 74.2% capacity after 5000 cycles at 2 C and Li|PL‐CEC|LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 (NCM811) cells deliver excellent cycling durability and high‐rate capability. Notably, multilayer Li|PL‐CEC|NCM811 pouch cell achieves Ah‐level capacity, demonstrating the practical scalability of PL‐CEC. This work establishes a molecular‐chain engineering strategy to enhance Li + transport and electrode interfacial stability for advanced SPEs toward long‐cycle SSLMBs.

title: Departing Pathways in Aza-Diarylethene Photoswitching: Elucidating the Role of the Central Ring Allows Reprogramming of the Photoresponse
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Aza-diarylethenes (aza-DAEs) are an emerging class of molecular photoswitches that allow reversible C–N bond formation and cleavage upon irradiation. They not only show high potential as T-type photochromes but also offer exciting opportunities for the exploration of unique reactivity control. Two types of these photoswitches are currently being investigated, which differ substantially in the nature of their metastable states. While classical DAE behavior is found in perfluorinated thiazole derivatives, an unexpected zwitterion formation and concomitant aromatization is observed for nonfluorinated pyrimidine derivatives. The latter offers reversible control over intramolecular charge separation and intrinsic three-state photoswitching. Their metastable state unleashes thiolate reactivity, which can be harnessed, e.g., in photoinitiation applications for smart polymer generation. Despite this promising progress, the reason for the divergent photochemical behavior in aza-DAEs is not yet understood. Here, we show that substitution of the central five-membered ring is responsible for the different photochemical outcomes and nature of the metastable state. Furthermore, our computational results provide systematic insights into the structural factors governing the relative stability of the neutral closed-ring and zwitterionic forms. We then use this knowledge to reprogram thioazole derivatives and render them into zwitterion-forming aza-DAEs. With these results, the predictable and rational design of aza-DAEs is enabled, which can now be radically changed in their photoresponses and tailored to specific desired properties and applications.

title: Halide‐Based Mixed Ionic‐Electronic Conductors Deliver High‐Rate and Long‐Life All‐Solid‐State Lithium Batteries
source: Advanced Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Interfacial side reactions and degradation of solid–solid contact limit the rate capability and cycling stability of composite cathodes in all‐solid‐state lithium batteries. Here, we introduce C5.5Mo (LiMo 2 O 2.75 Cl 5.5 ), a functional halide oxide additive designed to maintain solid–solid contact, improve charge transport, and regulate the composite‐cathode interface. Its mixed ionic‐electronic conductivity and low Young's modulus promote a dense cathode microstructure and stable interparticle contact during cycling. Bias‐dependent electrochemical impedance spectroscopy of composite‐cathode symmetric cells reveals lower interfacial resistance and reduced bias sensitivity, suggesting partial alleviation of space‐charge‐layer‐related transport limitations. The full‐cell system still provides a specific capacity of approximately 100 mAh g −1 at 6 C and maintains stable cycling for 20 000 cycles (capacity retention of 85.84%). This work establishes a practical additive strategy for constructing high‐rate and long‐life composite cathodes.

title: Immobilizing Ionomers by Strong Hydrogen Bonds for Highly Stable Industrial Water Electrolysis at 3.0 A/cm2
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Raising the operating current density can effectively reduce the high cost of proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs), but this approach is limited by rapid electrode degradation. Our previous research identified a critical degradation mechanism in which ionomer migration blocks mass-transport channels in the anode catalyst layer (ACL). Here, we find that each sulfonate group of the ionomer forms only about half a hydrogen bond on the IrO2 surface, indicating a weak catalyst–ionomer interaction. Rather than modifying the IrO2 surface, we propose to introduce additives that provide additional adsorption sites forming stronger hydrogen bonds (SHB) with the sulfonate groups. The resulting SHB-ACL maintains a stable ionomer distribution and pore network even after aging, and exhibits a roughly four fold lower degradation rate over 2500 h at 3.0 A/cm2. Furthermore, the electrode can be readily scaled up to 600 cm2. The improvement stability is at least in part attributable to enhanced interface interaction, although preserved porosity, water/gas transport, and interparticle contacts may also contribute. These findings offer a scalable route toward durable industrial PEMWE devices.

title: Electric vehicles as mobile energy carriers: An activity-based agent-based model of residential PV origin energy flows and V2G
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) is turning transportation management into a coupled mobility and energy planning problem. Public EVCS deployment affects travel behavior, parking duration, and local electricity demand, while EV batteries may also provide flexible storage through vehicle-to-grid (V2G) operation. However, the extent to which EVs can redistribute residential photovoltaic (PV) energy depends not only on charging infrastructure but also on daily activity schedules, state-of-charge conditions, dwell times, and station-side constraints. This study develops an activity-based agent-based model to evaluate EVs as mobile carriers of residential PV-origin energy in an urban charging system. The model links home charging, activity-based travel, public charging, V2G discharge, stationary battery energy storage systems, and charging station feasibility constraints. The framework is applied to Eindhoven, the Netherlands. Results show that EVs can acquire substantial residential PV-origin energy through home charging, but consume only about 6% of it during daily travel. Most PV-origin energy remains stored in EV batteries when vehicles arrive at non-home locations, creating technical potential for redistribution. However, activity context is the dominant bottleneck limiting V2G opportunities, indicating that urban V2G potential is shaped less by infrastructure availability alone than by when and where eligible EVs are parked during daily routines.

title: Cost-carbon preference reversals between new and second-life batteries in stationary storage: a long-horizon comparative framework
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: This paper develops a transparent, replacement-aware framework for comparing new battery systems (NBS) and second-life batteries (SLBs) in stationary-storage portfolios over a 30-year horizon. Five fixed portfolio compositions, three utilization profiles, and three grid‑carbon trajectories are evaluated using asset-side cost and carbon metrics. Unlike a pointwise techno-economic or environmental comparison, the framework is organized around the identification of conditional preference boundaries and the assessment of their robustness. The deterministic reference cases are complemented by alternative degradation and operation-and-maintenance formulations, a corrected replacement-threshold analysis, alternative first-life carbon-allocation and end-of-life conventions, two-parameter interaction maps, and a 10,000-sample simultaneous uncertainty analysis. The economic preference pattern remains unchanged across the tested structural formulations: SLB has the lowest asset-side levelized cost of storage under low and medium utilization, whereas NBS becomes preferable under high utilization. Under simultaneous uncertainty, the frequency with which SLB attains a lower asset-side cost decreases from 67.49% under low utilization to 40.66% under high utilization. The environmental ranking is more sensitive to the adopted accounting boundary. The reuse-oriented cutoff convention favors SLB across much of the reference space, but the preference can reverse when part of the first-life manufacturing burden and the end-of-life treatment of retired cohorts are included. The main contribution is therefore an integrated framework for identifying and robustness-testing economic and environmental preference boundaries between NBS and SLB, rather than prescribing a universally superior storage technology.
